item.title: A Red Dwarf is Taking its Time Eating a Brown Dwarf
item.description: Astronomers detected an unusual triangular light curve about 300 light years away. They were searching for Black Widow Binaries, where a dense neutron star eats its companion. But they found something different: an M dwarf slowly eating its binary companion brown dwarf.

item.title: Space waves reveal where Earth's magnetic shield is under pressure
item.description: A new study led by researchers at the University of Oulu in Finland sheds light on a poorly understood part of space weather: where powerful waves form at the edge of Earth's magnetic shield and where the solar wind can find a way through.

item.title: Hubble Spots a Suspected Second-Generation Planet
item.description: Diligent sleuthing by astronomers has broken open a cold case in the data archive of NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope. In a study published Monday in Nature Astronomy, researchers report uncovering a surprising chemical clue that indicates the white dwarf star HS 0209+0832 may host a second-generation planet.

item.title: Oct. 12, 1964: Voshkod 1 sends the first crew to space
item.description: Voshkod 1 kicked off the second series of manned Soviet spaceflights, following the Vostok missions that had been the first to put humans in space. item.title: Four astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
item.description: Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.

item.title: Astronomers pinpoint the most distant fast radio burst ever detected
item.description: Astronomers have detected and traced the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, a powerful flash of radio waves that traveled for more than 10 billion years across the cosmos before reaching Earth.

item.title: Largest 2D map of the universe helps scientists discover new gravitational lenses
item.description: Using data from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, with help from artificial intelligence, an international team of scientists has discovered 70 new gravitational lenses—rare cosmic alignments that act as natural magnifying glasses. The new lenses further expand one of the largest collections of confirmed lenses to date and will allow scientists to study dark matter, galaxy evolution and the structure of the universe.

item.title: Mission success: Australian cancer research returns from space
item.description: Human stem cells from Adelaide University's Center for Cancer Biology have successfully traveled to the edge of space and back as part of a landmark mission for Australian cancer research.

item.title: Thousands of Black Holes Could Be Lurking in Our Backyard—and You Can Help Find Them
item.description: According to stellar evolution models, there should be hundreds of millions of black holes floating around in our galaxy. But so far we’ve only found 70. item.title: A lack of rockets is creating a crisis for space technology companies
item.description: SpaceX’s changing priorities, the war in Ukraine and a lack of competitors are all causing a launch crisis that might last years

item.title: NASA demonstrates next-generation heat shield technologies
item.description: NASA is taking an unusual approach to testing heat shields that can keep astronauts safe as they return from missions to the moon and Mars: taking out the trash.

item.title: Is China catching up to the US and SpaceX on reusable rockets?
item.description: The next space race is not about making rockets faster, bigger or more capacious, but about reusing them reliably and cheaply. The US is well ahead, but can China catch up?

item.title: The next generation’s guide to the new space economy
item.description: An industry report published by students in an MIT aerospace entrepreneurship class lays out guidance for aspiring space leaders and investors.

item.title: SpaceX’s Starship will orbit Earth for first time during next flight
item.description: Starship's next test flight will be its first orbital mission. The craft will also release working Starlink V3 satellites for the first time, making the flight the first commercially useful Starship mission

item.title: How to design a space habitat that supports its residents’ mental health
item.description: A new online platform helps engineers look beyond survival mode when designing habitats for extreme living conditions.

item.title: Supporting mission-driven space innovation, for Earth and beyond
item.description: Aurelia Institute, founded by a team from MIT, serves as a research lab, an education and outreach center, and a policy hub for the space industry.

item.title: Turning up the heat on next-generation semiconductors
item.description: Research sheds light on the properties of novel materials that could be used in electronics operating in extremely hot environments.

item.title: Newly discovered Earth-sized planet may lack an atmosphere
item.description: Circling a cold, Jupiter-sized star, the new world could offer an unobstructed view of its surface composition and history.

item.title: Astronomers spot a giant planet that is as light as cotton candy
item.description: The new world is the second-lightest planet discovered to date.

item.title: Study: Life’s building blocks are surprisingly stable in Venus-like conditions
item.description: Results suggest the clouds of Venus could be hospitable for some forms of life.

item.title: A carbon-lite atmosphere could be a sign of water and life on other terrestrial planets, MIT study finds
item.description: A low carbon abundance in planetary atmospheres, which the James Webb Space Telescope can detect, could be a signature of habitability.

item.title: ALMA catches a dying star mid-transformation, with a ring from its last outburst
item.description: Astronomers have used radio observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to catch a dying star in the middle of a dramatic transformation, and the data show a ring that records its final outburst. The new research was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 18. The paper has been accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal.

item.title: Hypernovae May Be All Hype, No Nova
item.description: Astrophysicists think that hypernovae are the most powerful stellar explosions in the Universe. They're the most explosive type of core-collapse supernova. But the evidence for them is not voluminous, and new research pokes holes in it, pointing out that hypernovae may not actually exist.

item.title: Tiny Gold Nanogaps Could Crack the Chirality Puzzle
item.description: Looking for biosignatures across the solar system requires looking for asymmetry. Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, are famously either “left-handed” (L) or “right-handed” (D). We know abiotic processes (i.e. those that create amino acids but don’t involve life) create a 50/50 mixture of the two types, which is called a racemic mixture. item.title: Physics Nobel highlights Antarctica's role in exploring the cosmos
item.description: When Belgian American particle physicist Francis Halzen was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin," it was a reminder that for more than a century, scientists have treated Antarctica's environments as windows onto worlds beyond Earth.

item.title: Honda Wants to Put a Robotic Lab Assistant on Future Commercial Space Stations
item.description: As I’m writing this I’m able to stare out into my driveway at my trusty Honda Odyssey. Most of the public’s association with Honda is through their “mobility” products - i.e. their cars. But the company has an impressive track record of other technical achievements, not the least of which has been in robotics. Now, it’s teaming up with space infrastructure firm Redwire to develop an automated laboratory support system for use on future commercial space stations.
